title.full: Rescuing 1.5°C: New evidence on the highest possible ambition to deliver the Paris Agreement

publisher.full: Climate Analytics and Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research

description: Normative global REMIND pathway minimising 1.5°C overshoot from 2025; ~1.7°C peak, ~1.2°C in 2100.
pathwayDescription:
Climate Analytics is a climate science and policy institute that supports governments in meeting the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C limit and co-develops the Climate Action Tracker. The Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) is a leading climate research centre and develops the REMIND model used here. Together they published the Highest Possible Ambition (HPA) scenario in November 2025. Climate Analytics extended it to 13 countries and regions in 2026 through its 1.5°C national pathway explorer.
The HPA scenario asks how far global warming can be limited if every country pursues the highest possible climate ambition from 2025 onward. It is a normative pathway: after 2025, REMIND 3.5 is driven to the lowest carbon budget achievable within physical, technological and economic feasibility limits. Because insufficient action has made a temporary breach of 1.5°C unavoidable, the aim is to keep the overshoot as small and short as possible. Warming peaks at around 1.7°C and falls to about 1.2°C by 2100. Global CO2 emissions reach net zero in 2045 and total greenhouse gases in 2060. The scenario updates the IPCC AR6 1.5°C pathways to today's higher starting emissions and the faster-than-expected fall in clean technology costs.
Four main drivers shape the pathway. First, carbon pricing is the single modelled policy instrument, used as a proxy for overall regulatory effort. Prices are higher in richer regions so that advanced economies cut emissions faster, and converge to a uniform global price by 2070. Second, falling technology costs make wind, solar and batteries the cheapest option: solar PV capital costs fall by two-thirds by 2050, and electricity reaches nearly two-thirds of final energy. Third, low-carbon energy investment rises from 1.4% to a peak of about 4.2% of GDP in 2035, led by power, storage and grids; renewable investment peaks first in advanced economies and around 2040 in emerging ones. Finally, an energy-equity adjustment cuts energy use per person by 25% in advanced economies and raises it by 25% in low-income regions by 2040. Caps on biomass and geological CO2 storage limit reliance on carbon removal, while GDP and population follow the middle-of-the-road SSP2 trajectory.

coreDrivers.policies: Carbon pricing is the single modelled policy instrument. Carbon prices are higher in developped regions so advanced economies cut emissions faster, and every region reaches the same price by 2070. The authors treat the price as a proxy for overall regulatory effort, not a prescription for carbon pricing alone. Up to 2025 emissions follow the current-policy trajectory.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: The pathway aims to minimize emissions. After 2025, the model is driven to the lowest carbon budget achievable within its techno-economic constraints, to limit 1.5°C overshoot and return warming below 1.5°C before 2100. This yields net zero CO2 in 2045 and net zero GHG in 2060.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: REMIND is an intertemporal cost-optimising model, so unit costs decide which technologies supply the carbon-budget-constrained energy system. Falling costs make wind, solar and batteries the cheapest option, driving electrification to nearly two-thirds of final energy by 2050. Solar PV capital cost falls 66% (2025-2050), onshore wind 36%, electrolysers 82%, while fossil plant costs stay flat. The report credits renewables' faster-than-expected cost decline for the steeper cuts versus AR6.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-carbon energy-supply investment rises from 1.37% of GDP (2025) to a peak of 4.15% (2035), then eases to 2.20% (2050), led by non-fossil power, storage and grids. Nationally, renewable power investment peaks in 2026-2030 in advanced economies (EU, Germany, UK, US), and around 2040 in least developed economies as Brazil, India and Colombia, consistent with higher near-term carbon prices in richer regions.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: GDP and population follow the SSP2 'middle-of-the-road' trajectory (population reaches 9.6 billion and GDP US$155 trillion MER by 2050), which sets underlying energy-service and food demand. The report links continued growth in animal-protein and waste-related demand under SSP2 to the slower methane cuts in agriculture and waste.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: The scenario imposes an energy-equity adjustment from outside the model. Compared with current policies, energy use per person is cut by 25% in advanced economies and raised by 25% in low-income regions. This change is phased in gradually between 2025 and 2040. Sustainability caps bind the supply side: biomass is capped to 80 EJ/yr and geological CO2 storage to 8.6 GtCO2/yr, limiting BECCS and leaving little room for fossil CCS. Optimistic methane abatement cost curves are used.

dependencies.dependency_description: Critical: The pathway needs every country to put highest-possible-ambition targets into NDCs and long-term strategies, revisit net-zero dates, and coordinate internationally. The most concrete power-sector milestone is renewable capacity reaching ~12 TW by 2030, more than tripling from 2022 and above the COP28 tripling goal; this delivers nearly 40% of 2030 emissions cuts. The authors state the 2030s transformation is not possible without this policy commitment.
not applicable.

High: Carbon prices, highest in richer regions, make fossil plants uneconomic, forcing around 200 GW/yr of fossil capacity retirements in 2025-2035, about double the AR6 average, with greater asset stranding. Annual power investment rises from US$1.4 trillion (2025) to US$4.6 trillion (2035). The authors note equitable delivery would need international support including financial transfers to developing regions.
not applicable.

Low: Electricity demand roughly quadruples as end uses electrify, but this is modelled as cost-driven substitution, not consumer choice. The one demand-side assumption, a 25% cut in per-capita final energy in advanced economies (and +25% in low-income regions), is imposed exogenously and the authors do not say whether it comes from efficiency or changed consumption. It shifts electricity demand but is not described as a constraint.

Critical: The authors call adequate grids and flexibility the cornerstone of keeping 1.5°C alive. Storage capacity grows from 112 GW (2025) to 17151 GW (2050), and grid investment from US$641bn to a peak of US$2140bn a year (2040). Curtailment reaches 12% of generation by 2050, a sign of integration stress. REMIND is annual and does not report hourly dispatch, so flexibility needs cannot be checked against a time-resolved profile.

High: Battery storage must scale from near zero to ~17,000 GW by 2050 to firm variable renewables. BECCS in power reaches only ~15 GW, but it belongs to an engineered-removal sector the authors call unprecedented. Hydrogen-fired generation appears as a small firming source. Fossil CCS stays marginal (~6 GW) because limited CO2 storage is prioritised for removals and industry. No efficiency ceilings are discussed for power technologies.

Moderate: Two caps bind the power mix. Biomass supply is limited to around 80 EJ/yr to avoid land, food and biodiversity conflicts, and geological CO2 storage to 8.6 GtCO2 per year. Together they keep BECCS power small and fossil CCS marginal, so power decarbonisation rests on wind, solar and storage. The authors note sustainable biomass could be as low as 30-50 EJ per year, which would tighten the constraint.
not applicable.
not applicable.

Low: No steel-specific policy is identified. Steel decarbonises under the economy-wide, regionally differentiated carbon price, and the report's policy recommendations (NDC ambition, renewables tripling, net-zero dates) are economy-wide. The shift from blast furnaces to EAF and hydrogen DRI is described as an outcome, not as following a sectoral roadmap.
not applicable.

Cannot assess: The economy-wide carbon price is the only economic condition reaching steel, and steel CO2 falls to zero by 2050. The report gives no steel-specific cost, profitability, green-premium or financing information, so whether economics constrain the EAF and hydrogen-DRI switch cannot be judged.
not applicable.

Low: The exogenous 25% per-capita final-energy cut in advanced economies may partly come from lower demand for consumer goods, which would cut industrial output, but the authors leave the mix open. Steel final energy falls 32% from 2025 to 2050. No green premium or buyer behaviour is discussed.

Moderate: Steel switches to hydrogen and electricity: hydrogen supplies 54% and electricity 46% of steel final energy by 2050, with coal eliminated. This needs hydrogen supply and clean-power connections at steel sites. Evidence-based inference: the report shows the fuel switch but does not discuss steel-site infrastructure or regional siting.

High: Steel decarbonisation depends on hydrogen direct reduction, not yet at commercial scale: hydrogen use in steel rises from 0.15 EJ (2025) to 12.9 EJ (2050) as blast furnaces are replaced by EAF and hydrogen DRI. Industrial CCS is not allocated to steel. The report gives no technology readiness or cost milestones for hydrogen DRI.
not applicable.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Derived, not reported: row 210 Emissions|CO2|Energy|Supply|Electricity / row 523 Secondary Energy|Electricity (EJ -> TWh). Direct CO2 only, net of BECCS, so it turns negative by 2050 (-0.7 g/kWh). Global system; no on-grid/captive/rooftop split.

Net direct CO2 from electricity supply, including BECCS removals (row 210); gross CO2 without removals also reported (row 429). CO2 only, no CH4/N2O for power. Global system; no on-grid/captive/rooftop split.

Installed capacity in GW. Storage (row 41) is one GW figure not split by technology; the report names battery storage but does not say whether pumped hydro is included. Storage additions also in GWh/yr (row 18). 'Other' (row 37) is undescribed, likely hydrogen turbines. No on-grid/captive/rooftop split.

Secondary Energy|Electricity in EJ/yr (convert x 277.78 for TWh). Curtailment reported separately (row 530: 49.7 EJ in 2050); the dataset does not say whether totals are net of it. Hydrogen-fired generation not reported as its own row. No on-grid/captive/rooftop split.
Derived: generation by technology (rows 524-544) / total (row 523). Unallocated residual (~2% in 2050, likely hydrogen) not attributable. Report Fig. 7b gives shares as a chart only.
Overnight capital cost per kW by technology (rows 60-72) in US$2010. No O&M, fuel cost, LCOE or storage cost.

granularity: By tech, part of value chain
byMetric.scopeLimitations: Annual investment in billion US$2010/yr, global. Excludes upstream fuel supply (reported separately under energy supply, rows 468-473).

granularity: High-carbon assets lifetime face early retirement policy
byMetric.scopeLimitations: No plant-level lifetimes reported; retirement inferred from net capacity decline (coal 2,033 -> 698 GW, gas 1,970 -> 1,149 GW, 2025-2035) and Fig. 11 rates.

Energy-related direct CO2 from iron and steel (row 202); excludes process CO2 (not reported for steel) and indirect electricity emissions. Ironmaking and steelmaking modelled together; cannot be separated.
